Attacking & Defending an ICS/SCADA Environment

A guided walk through one lab scenario: an attacker pivots from Kali to the engineering station, touches the Windows domain and the PLC network, while Malcolm SIEM and pfSense give the blue team the visibility to detect and hunt it.

Lab use only. Everything here ran in an isolated virtual range with an emulated PLC (Studio 5000 Logix Emulate). The course focuses on understanding, observing and detecting each stage. Never test against systems you do not own or have written authorization to assess.
MODULE 0

Start here: objectives, lab setup & rules of engagement

Learning objectives

  • Describe the plant process and what a cyber incident could affect
  • Map an ICS attack path to the Purdue Model and ATT&CK for ICS
  • Read captures, firewall, Windows and SIEM evidence together
  • Write and test two detections; produce an incident report

Prerequisites

  • TCP/IP, DNS and basic firewall concepts
  • Windows administration and Event Viewer
  • Linux shell basics (Kali)
  • No PLC programming experience needed

Before every session

  • Snapshots: take a clean snapshot of every VM; revert after each run so results are repeatable.
  • Time sync: point every system (Kali, Windows, pfSense, Malcolm) at one NTP source and use one time zone. Your screenshots mix EST and UTC, which makes timelines hard to prove. Check with w32tm /query /status on Windows and timedatectl on Linux.
  • Isolation: the range must have no path to production or the internet except what you intend.
  • Sanitise screenshots: remove real project names, usernames, hostnames and saved-password tabs before sharing the course.
Rules of engagement. Work only inside the written scope of this range. Use only the accounts you are given. Do not touch real production equipment. Do not change PLC logic, forces or setpoints in the exercises; discuss impact, do not cause it. Stop immediately and tell the instructor if something outside the range responds or the process behaves unexpectedly.
MODULE 1

The process under protection: HMI & utilities

Objectives: read the plant overview, understand what a cyber incident could affect, and learn the normal baseline before hunting for abnormal.

The target is a membrane bioreactor (MBR) wastewater plant: screened influent goes through a flow splitter box into two anoxic/aerobic trains, then through ultrafiltration (UF) membranes whose permeate leaves to the permeate tank. The SCADA HMI shows each train’s flow, turbidity, TMP (transmembrane pressure), mode and sequence step.

What an attacker could target

  • Setpoints and operating mode of UF trains
  • Chemical dosing: hypochlorite, citric acid, sodium hydroxide
  • Alarm acknowledgement and reset to hide faults

What a defender records

  • Normal flows, modes, and operator login levels
  • Which hosts legitimately talk to the PLC
  • Fault states that already exist (avoid false attribution)
MODULE 2

Lab topology & scenario kill chain

Objectives: map each tool in the screenshots to a zone and follow the attack path that the rest of the course walks through.

Red dashed = attack path · teal dotted = telemetry to Malcolm. Addresses are taken from the lab screenshots; adapt to your own range.

Purdue Model mapping

The Purdue Model (ISA-95 / ISA-99 zones and conduits) splits an industrial site into levels. Traffic should move level by level through controlled conduits, so a compromise at the top cannot reach the process at the bottom unnoticed. Here is where each lab component sits:

LEVEL 5
Enterprise / InternetKali attacker, 192.168.91.129 (starting foothold)
LEVEL 4
Site business / ITWindows domain: AD DS, DNS, file and IIS services (172.16.0.2 / 192.168.169.252); pfSense’s IT-side interface also lives here
LEVEL 4 / 3.5 · IDMZ
Industrial DMZ, the IT/OT boundary. The firewall straddles Level 4 and Level 3.5pfSense firewall: IT-facing interface 192.168.91.254 (Level 4), DMZ interface (Level 3.5), OT interface toward Level 3; logs forwarded to Malcolm
LEVEL 3
Site operationsEngineering station (192.168.100.10), Malcolm SIEM and sensor
LEVEL 2
Supervisory controlHMI / SCADA (FactoryTalk), the screens in Module 1
LEVEL 1
Basic controlPLC, Logix Emulate (192.168.100.40, EtherNet/IP)
LEVEL 0
Physical processUF membranes, pumps, blowers, valves, air compressors, instruments

Placement follows common practice and the addresses in your screenshots. Adjust it to how your range is actually wired, for example whether the engineering station and Malcolm sit in Level 3 or a dedicated Level 2 engineering zone.

Where the lab breaks the model

  • Multi-homed attacker: Kali has an interface on 192.168.100.x (OT) and another on 192.168.91.x, so it skips the IDMZ completely.
  • Direct SSH from Level 5/4 to a Level 3 host: no jump host, no protocol break.
  • Dual-homed domain controller: one identity system spans IT and OT networks, so stolen credentials travel across levels.
  • Engineering station reaches Level 1: compromise of Level 3 gives legitimate-looking CIP access to the PLC.

Detect and enforce at each conduit

  • 5/4 → 3.5: pfSense default-deny, alert on any new source to OT ranges
  • 3.5 → 3: allow-list SSH/RDP from a jump host only, with MFA
  • 3 → 2/1: allow EtherNet/IP only from engineering station and HMI
  • 1 → 0: controller mode, force and download monitoring
  • Malcolm sensors on the mirror ports of each conduit

Scenario kill chain (MITRE ATT&CK for ICS)

Read the chain against the Purdue levels: each step below crosses or tests a boundary, from Level 5/4 down toward Level 1.

Recon of OT subnet
T0846 Remote System Discovery
Sniff controller traffic
T0842 Network Sniffing
SSH into engineering station
T0886 Remote Services
Use harvested credentials / domain
T0859 Valid Accounts
Reach PLC via engineering software

Impact on process

Click a step above to see the Purdue levels it touches (highlighted in the stack above) and how to detect it.

In this course stages 1–4 are exercised and observed. Stages 5–6 are discussed as impact potential only, so that students understand why the detections in Modules 7–8 matter.

MODULE 3

PLC logic & the engineering station

Objectives: understand what lives on the engineering station, why it is the crown jewel, and what “normal” engineering activity looks like.

The PLC program (PLC_506922_ThompsonStation_R0) is open in Logix Designer on an emulated 5570 controller. The task tree shows UFX sequence routines: master cycle, rotation, setpoints, motors, valves, alarms and analogs.

Defender takeaways

  • Whoever controls this workstation can change logic, forces and setpoints. Treat it as Tier 0.
  • Alert on Run → Program mode changes, forces enabled, and downloads from any host other than the engineering station.
  • Keep known-good project backups and hashes to compare.
MODULE 4

Attacker workstation: Kali and the SSH pivot

Objectives: recognise the footprint of reconnaissance and remote-access pivoting from the attacker’s side so you can detect it from the defender’s side.

Attacker view

  • Enumerate local interfaces and routes to find the OT segment
  • Probe industrial ports (EtherNet/IP 44818, 2222)
  • Use SSH with reused or weak credentials to land on a trusted host

Defender view

  • New SSH (TCP 22) sessions into the engineering VLAN
  • Windows logon events 4624/4625 and OpenSSH service logs
  • Disable or restrict SSH on engineering hosts; use a jump host with MFA
MODULE 5

Seeing the wire: Wireshark & NetworkMiner

Objectives: read industrial and support traffic, tell chatter from conversation, and build a baseline of who talks to whom.
ObservationLikely meaningHunt idea
UDP 1947 broadcasts from .100.10TO VERIFYLicence discovery on the engineering stationAlert if another host starts emitting it
UDP 4445→4446 to 231.1.1.1TO VERIFYEmulator/chassis multicast heartbeatBaseline source and interval
TCP 44818 / UDP 2222EtherNet/IP (CIP) explicit / implicit messagingAllow-list: only the engineering station and HMI
MODULE 6

Domain controller: the identity bridge between IT and OT

Objectives: understand why a Windows domain inside or next to OT widens the blast radius, and which events reveal abuse.

Why it matters

  • Engineering-station admin rights usually come from domain groups
  • Compromised domain credentials open every joined HMI and server
  • Dual-homed DC bridges the OT and enterprise ranges

Detections

  • 4624 type 3/10 logons to the engineering station from Kali’s IP
  • 4768/4769 Kerberos anomalies, 4720/4728 account or group changes
  • Tiering: separate OT admin accounts, no domain admins on HMIs
MODULE 7

Malcolm SIEM: monitor, triage and hunt

Objectives: use Malcolm’s dashboards (Zeek + Suricata on OpenSearch) to turn the earlier activity into findings.

Where Malcolm should listen

Malcolm sees only what reaches its capture interface. Mirror (SPAN) traffic from these points, and compare against the empty OT Devices panel:

  • The switch port of the PLC and engineering station: EtherNet/IP and engineering software traffic.
  • The pfSense OT and DMZ interfaces: everything that crosses a zone boundary.
  • The domain controller uplink: Kerberos, LDAP and SMB.

Loopback and same-host traffic never reaches a sensor. Ensure the ICS protocol parsers are enabled, and send host and firewall logs as a second source.

Hunting workflow

  1. Scope: filter event.severity:* and the last 24 h.
  2. Pivot: from “Connection attempt, no reply” to source IPs, then to destination ports 44818/2222/22.
  3. Compare: does the source appear in the asset inventory as an allowed engineering host?
  4. Correlate: match with DC logons and firewall logs in the same window.
  5. Report: time, hosts, evidence, ATT&CK technique, recommendation.

Starter searches (Lucene, Dashboards bar)

Field names can differ between Malcolm versions; confirm them in the field list on the left of Discover.

destination.port:44818 AND NOT source.ip:(192.168.100.10 OR <HMI_IP>)
destination.port:22 AND destination.ip:192.168.100.*
event.severity:[40 TO *]
event.dataset:notice

Query 1 flags any host other than the engineering station and HMI speaking EtherNet/IP. Query 2 finds SSH into the OT range. Query 3 lists the higher-severity tags. Save each as a saved search and alert on it.

MODULE 8

pfSense firewall: segmentation and log forwarding

Objectives: enforce the IT/OT boundary and feed the firewall’s view of the traffic to Malcolm.

Where pfSense belongs: Level 4 and Level 3.5

The firewall is the conduit between the business network (Level 4) and the industrial DMZ (Level 3.5), and it then guards the entrance to the operations zone (Level 3). It should therefore have one interface in each zone, so that no traffic goes from IT to OT without passing through the DMZ.

pfSense interfacePurdue levelLab addressRule intent
LAN / ITLevel 4192.168.91.254 CONFIRMEDOnly brokered requests into the DMZ; deny direct access to OT ranges
OPT1 / IDMZLevel 3.510.35.0.1/24 FICTIONAL
Jump host 10.35.0.10 · patch/AV relay 10.35.0.20 · data mirror 10.35.0.30		Hosts the jump host, patch/AV relay and data mirror; the only place IT and OT sessions terminate
OPT2 / OTLevel 3 and below192.168.100.254/24 FICTIONAL
Engineering station .100.10 · PLC .100.40		Allow-list EtherNet/IP, SSH/RDP from the jump host only; log all denies
  • Placement rule: traffic between Level 4 and Level 3 is never allowed to go straight through; it must stop in the DMZ at Level 3.5.
  • Optional hardening: use two firewalls (IT-to-DMZ and DMZ-to-OT), ideally from different vendors, so one bug cannot open both boundaries.
  • Lab gap: Kali has a leg on 192.168.100.x, so the OT side is reachable without crossing the firewall. Remove it to test the placement.

Hardening

  • Default-deny between IT, DMZ and OT; allow-list by host and port
  • Block management access from user/attacker segments
  • Alias lists for PLC, HMI and engineering IPs

Send logs to Malcolm

  • Status → System Logs → Settings → Remote Logging: point to Malcolm’s syslog listener
  • Optionally mirror an OT port (SPAN) to Malcolm’s capture interface
  • Confirm in Malcolm that the pfSense source appears under Log Source
MODULE 9

Hunt checklist & knowledge check

Hunt checklist

  • Any new host talking EtherNet/IP to the PLC?
  • New SSH sessions into the engineering VLAN?
  • Logons by domain admins on HMIs?
  • Controller mode, forces, or program downloads changed?
  • Firewall rule changes or admin logins from non-management IPs?
  • Gaps: OT Devices panel empty, capture-loss notices.

Lab exercises

  • Baseline 24 h of traffic, then repeat the Kali recon and compare.
  • Write a Malcolm saved search for TCP 44818 from non-allow-listed IPs.
  • Draft an incident report for the SSH pivot with ATT&CK mapping.

Q1. Why is the engineering station the highest-value pivot target?

It can change PLC logic and setpoints, and its traffic to the controller looks legitimate.

Q2. Why does a VirusTotal lookup of 192.168.100.10 return “clean”?

It is a private address; public feeds have no meaningful data. Use internal asset inventory and baselines.

Q3. Which TCP port is used by EtherNet/IP explicit messaging?

44818 (UDP 2222 for implicit I/O).

Q4. The nmap check of 127.0.0.1:44818 on Kali never appears in Malcolm. Why?

Loopback traffic stays inside the host and never crosses a mirrored network path, so only host logging sees it.

Q5. The “OT Devices” panel shows no results. What does that tell you?

Malcolm has not identified any device through its ICS protocol parsers: either the PLC traffic is not reaching the sensor or the protocol is not being parsed. Fix visibility before trusting the dashboards.

Q6. Name two Windows events that show a remote logon to the engineering station.

4624 (successful logon, types 3 or 10) and 4625 (failed logon); also 4648 for explicit credentials.

Q7. Why is a default admin account on the boundary firewall a problem even in a lab?

Whoever reaches the GUI can alter segmentation and delete evidence. Rename or restrict it, limit GUI access to a management host and log changes.

Q8. Which ATT&CK for ICS technique covers capturing controller traffic with Wireshark?

T0842 Network Sniffing.

MODULE 10

Hands-on labs, response & hardening

Objectives: practise detection end to end, respond without disrupting the process, and close the gaps found in earlier modules. Run all labs only in the authorised range.
Lab 1 · Build a traffic baseline (30 min)

Steps

  1. Capture 15 minutes on the OT adapter with the plant idle.
  2. List talkers in NetworkMiner (Hosts tab) and Malcolm (VADR Inventory).
  3. Record every periodic source, destination, port and interval.

Checkpoint

Which host sends UDP 1947 broadcasts and how often?

Solution

In the sample capture: 192.168.100.10, in pairs about every 0.23 s. Your numbers become the baseline for Lab 3.

Lab 2 · Detect the SSH pivot (45 min)

Steps

  1. From Kali, open an SSH session to the engineering station (authorised lab account).
  2. On the station, list recent logons:
    Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security';Id=4624,4625;StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} |
  Select TimeCreated,Id,@{n='Msg';e={$_.Message.Split("`n")[0..20] -join ' '}}
  3. Check the OpenSSH operational log and the pfSense firewall log for TCP 22.
  4. In Malcolm search destination.port:22 AND destination.ip:192.168.100.*.

Checkpoint

Which three data sources recorded the session, and which one would you lose if the host were compromised?

Solution

Windows security log, firewall log, Zeek conn/ssh log. The host log can be wiped by the attacker, so network and firewall copies are your evidence.

Lab 3 · Alert on an unlisted EtherNet/IP client (60 min)

Steps

  1. Add one detection (Suricata or Zeek) from below to the sensor.
  2. From Kali, make a plain TCP connection test to the PLC on 44818 (for example an nmap port check).
  3. Confirm the alert appears in Malcolm and that the engineering station’s own traffic does not alert.
# Suricata (define ENG_HMI and PLC address groups first)
alert tcp !$ENG_HMI any -> $PLC 44818 (msg:"Unlisted EtherNet/IP client to PLC"; flow:to_server; sid:9000001; rev:1;)

# Zeek
@load base/frameworks/notice
redef enum Notice::Type += { ENIP_Unlisted_Client };
const allowed: set[addr] = { 192.168.100.10 } &redef;
event connection_state_remove(c: connection) {
  if ( c$id$resp_p == 44818/tcp && c$id$orig_h !in allowed )
    NOTICE([$note=ENIP_Unlisted_Client, $conn=c,
            $msg=fmt("Unlisted EtherNet/IP client %s", c$id$orig_h)]);
}

Checkpoint

Why must the allow-list come from Lab 1 and not a guess?

Solution

A wrong list either misses attackers or floods analysts with false positives. The baseline proves who is legitimate.

Lab 4 · Firewall rule and log forwarding to Malcolm (30 min)

Steps

  1. pfSense → Firewall → Rules: block 192.168.91.0/24 to 192.168.100.0/24 on TCP 22 and 44818, tick Log packets.
  2. Status → System Logs → Settings: enable remote logging to Malcolm’s syslog address.
  3. Trigger the rule from Kali, then find it in Malcolm.

Checkpoint

What do you learn from a blocked-and-logged attempt that you would miss with a silent drop?

Solution

Source, destination and timing of reconnaissance, which is early warning before anything succeeds.

What belongs in the Level 3.5 DMZ

  • Jump host with MFA: the only way to open SSH/RDP sessions into OT.
  • Patch and antivirus relay: OT systems fetch updates from here, never from the internet.
  • Historian or data mirror: IT reads plant data from the copy, not from live OT.
  • Remote access gateway: vendor and VPN sessions end here, are recorded, and are approved per request.

Remote access and safety systems

Remote access risk

  • Vendor VPN and remote desktop are a common real-world way in.
  • Shared accounts and always-on tunnels remove accountability.

Safety layers at Level 0/1

  • Safety instrumented systems and hard interlocks limit what a cyber attack can do to the process.
  • Keep them on a separate network and exclude them from the exercises.

Incident response in an OT environment

Do

  • Call the plant operator first; safety and process stability outrank forensics.
  • Contain at the conduits: block the attacker’s source at pfSense, disable the SSH account.
  • Preserve evidence: PCAP, Windows logs, firewall logs, project file hashes.
  • Prepare manual operation for the affected train.

Avoid

  • Power-cycling PLCs or the engineering station without a plan.
  • Scanning the production controller to “check” it.
  • Pushing a fresh program before comparing with a known-good backup.
  • Clearing logs or rebooting before images are taken.

Capstone exercise (90 min)

Task: after the range is reset and clocks are synchronised, one student runs the Module 4 steps (port check of the PLC, then the SSH session to the engineering station). Teams in the blue role must:
  1. Find the activity in at least three sources (firewall, Windows, Malcolm).
  2. Build one timeline in UTC with evidence links.
  3. Map it to Purdue levels and ATT&CK for ICS techniques.
  4. Write a one-page incident report using the Module 9 template.
  5. Propose five prioritised controls from the hardening checklist.
Marking: evidence quality 40 %, timeline accuracy 20 %, mapping 20 %, recommendations 20 %.

Instructor guide

Duration: 6–8 h (modules 1–9 about 3 h, labs about 3 h). Prerequisites: TCP/IP basics, Windows administration, basic Linux shell. Outcomes: map an ICS incident to the Purdue Model and ATT&CK for ICS; read captures and SIEM dashboards; write and test two detections; produce an incident report. Assessment: quiz (30 %), Labs 2–4 (40 %), incident report (30 %).
